This text describes improvements to a high-speed, smooth tool path designed primarily for finishing walls within bounded regions of virtually any shape. The improved tool path is especially useful in machining operations where clean, accurate wall finishes are required while maintaining efficient cutter movement.

The tool path can be used to finish both straight and drafted walls. In particular, it is effective for removing excess material left behind by a previous cutter with a larger diameter. After the larger tool has performed an earlier machining operation, smaller amounts of stock may remain along the walls or in tighter regions. The improved path allows a finishing cutter to remove this remaining material smoothly and accurately, producing the desired wall geometry.

Although the method is mainly intended for finishing, the same tool-motion strategy can also be applied to roughing operations. In roughing, the walls of the bounded region may be approximated by creating inward offsets from the original boundary. These offset curves guide the tool in progressively removing material while preserving the general shape of the desired wall.

Instead of simply offsetting the finished boundaries inward and cutting them at a constant cutter speed, the technique uses optimized cutting methods. These methods are intended to improve efficiency, reduce unnecessary motion, and maintain smoother tool movement. By optimizing the tool path rather than relying on constant speed alone, the machining process can become faster and more effective while still producing high-quality results.

Overall, the technique reduces wasted tool motion and improves machining efficiency. It can be applied to both closed and open bounded areas and is suitable for a wide range of wall geometries, including straight, drafted, and more complex boundary shapes. As a result, it provides a flexible and efficient approach for both finishing and roughing operations in high-speed machining.

counterfactuals.output:
A CAM machining method can generate optimized roughing and finishing tool paths by starting from the finished boundary of a bounded machining area and creating a series of inward offset curves.

The method works for both open and closed regions. The final desired part boundary is used as the reference contour, and successive inward offsets are computed at distances related to the cutter size, stepover, and remaining stock requirements. These offset curves define smooth, continuous machining passes inside the bounded area.

For roughing, the system removes material by following progressively offset paths that maintain a controlled engagement with the workpiece. This helps avoid abrupt direction changes, excessive cutter loading, and inefficient air cutting. The offsets can be adjusted or trimmed to respect islands, walls, open edges, and other boundary constraints.

For finishing, one or more final offset or boundary-following passes are generated closer to the finished contour, leaving or removing a specified stock allowance. Because the paths are derived from smooth offsets of the final geometry, the resulting motion is more continuous and produces better surface quality.

Overall, the method uses inward boundary offsets to automatically create efficient, smooth, and geometry-aware tool paths for machining bounded areas, improving cutting consistency, reducing tool wear, and supporting both rough material removal and final finishing operations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description for a manufacturing invention involving high-speed tool motion for finishing n-sided pockets or regions, reducing wasted cutter movement, and handling straight or drafted walls.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Description

The invention relates to computer-controlled machining methods and systems for high-speed finishing of pockets, cavities, islands, or other bounded regions having an arbitrary number of sides. More particularly, the invention provides a toolpath generation technique for finishing n-sided regions while reducing non-cutting cutter motion and accommodating both substantially vertical walls and drafted or tapered walls.

In conventional pocket finishing, cutter paths are often generated as a succession of offsets from a boundary, raster passes, or contour-parallel passes. Such approaches may create excessive linking moves, redundant traversal, sharp direction changes, or areas of cutter engagement that are not optimized for high-speed machining. These inefficiencies become more significant in pockets or regions having three, four, five, or more sides, especially where the boundary includes non-parallel segments, curved corner blends, islands, or variable wall draft. The invention addresses these limitations by generating a coordinated high-speed finishing pattern that maintains continuous cutter engagement and minimizes wasted cutter travel.

According to one embodiment, a machining region is defined by a closed boundary having n sides, where n is any integer greater than or equal to three. The boundary may be polygonal, may include curved segments, or may be represented by a CAD/CAM surface or solid model. The region may define a pocket bottom, a sidewall surface, a floor-wall transition, an island-bounded region, or a localized finish-machining area. The method receives or determines geometric data including the region boundary, the desired stock allowance, cutter geometry, stepover, scallop height, wall angle, depth of cut, and machine tool dynamic limits such as feed rate, acceleration, jerk, and cornering capability.

A toolpath generator constructs a plurality of finishing passes within the n-sided region. The finishing passes are arranged to follow the general shape of the region while avoiding unnecessary repositioning between passes. In one implementation, the path is generated from a medial, skeletal, morphing, or blended reference curve derived from the boundary. Successive passes may be formed by interpolation between opposing sides, by inward or outward morphing of boundary contours, or by dividing the region into subregions that can each be machined with continuous or near-continuous cutter motion. The resulting path may comprise spiral, trochoidal, contour-parallel, morph-parallel, or hybrid high-speed segments.

The invention reduces wasted cutter movement by selecting link moves that remain within or adjacent to the material-removal region whenever possible. Rather than retracting and repositioning between every pass, the system connects adjacent cutting passes using smooth transition curves, such as arcs, splines, clothoids, polynomial blends, or other curvature-continuous links. These transition curves may be selected to satisfy maximum curvature, feed-rate, acceleration, and jerk constraints of the machine tool. The cutter therefore remains engaged in productive or near-productive motion for a greater portion of the cycle, reducing air cutting and improving surface consistency.

For n-sided pockets, the method may identify side pairs, corner zones, and transition zones. In a quadrilateral region, for example, tool motion may be morphed between opposing wall boundaries. In a triangular or pentagonal region, the system may subdivide the pocket into machining sectors or generate a continuous path that progressively transitions among all sides. In more complex n-sided regions, the method may use a graph or topology-based representation of the pocket to determine an ordered sequence of cutting passes that covers the region with minimal overlap and minimal non-cutting displacement. The sequence may be optimized according to a cost function that penalizes retracts, long rapid moves, abrupt heading changes, excessive cutter engagement, and deviation from desired scallop height.

The technique is applicable to pockets or regions having straight walls. For straight-wall finishing, the toolpath may maintain a substantially constant lateral offset from the wall boundary at a given depth, thereby producing a uniform sidewall finish. Multiple axial levels may be machined using repeated or adjusted finishing paths, or a single helical or ramped path may be used where machine and tool constraints permit. The system may also compensate for cutter radius, corner radius, tool taper, tool deflection, and desired remaining stock.

The technique is further applicable to drafted walls. For drafted or tapered sidewalls, the boundary of the machining region changes as a function of height or depth. The invention determines a family of depth-dependent boundary curves corresponding to the wall draft angle or to the actual modeled wall surface. Toolpath passes are then adjusted at each axial level so that the cutter maintains the intended contact relationship with the drafted wall. In one embodiment, the path is offset laterally as depth changes according to the draft angle. In another embodiment, the path is generated directly from surface contact curves, thereby allowing accurate finishing of planar draft faces, curved draft faces, ruled surfaces, or blended wall-floor transitions.

When machining drafted walls, the method may produce a continuous three-dimensional toolpath in which the cutter moves simultaneously in X, Y, and Z. The path may follow a ramped, spiral, or morphing trajectory that maintains a target scallop height on the drafted surface. Smooth linking between levels reduces dwell marks and avoids visible witness lines. The system may also orient the tool axis for three-axis, four-axis, or five-axis machining, depending on the available machine configuration and the desired surface finish.

In some embodiments, the invention includes adaptive feed-rate control. Cutter engagement may be estimated along the generated path based on local geometry, remaining stock, cutter diameter, and stepover. Feed rates may be increased in low-engagement regions and reduced in high-engagement corner or transition regions. The method may also modify local stepover, path curvature, or linking geometry to prevent overload and maintain a desired chip thickness. This is particularly advantageous in high-speed finishing, where smooth motion and stable engagement are important for surface quality and tool life.

The generated toolpath may include one or more of the following features:

1. **Continuous or near-continuous finishing motion** within an n-sided pocket or bounded region.  
2. **Reduced retracts and rapid repositioning moves** by smoothly connecting adjacent cutting passes.  
3. **Boundary-morphed path generation** for regions having nonparallel or irregular sides.  
4. **Curvature-continuous transition links** suitable for high-speed machining.  
5. **Support for arbitrary n-sided geometries**, including triangular, quadrilateral, pentagonal, polygonal, curved, or hybrid boundaries.  
6. **Machining of straight walls** using constant-offset finishing paths.  
7. **Machining of drafted walls** using depth-dependent boundary offsets or surface-derived contact curves.  
8. **Optional subdivision of complex regions** into optimized subregions for efficient tool coverage.  
9. **Feed-rate and engagement optimization** to maintain stable high-speed cutting conditions.  
10. **Three-dimensional finishing paths** for tapered, drafted, or blended wall surfaces.

The invention may be implemented as software stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by a processor of a CAM system, CNC controller, or manufacturing planning system. The software receives geometric model data, machining parameters, and tool data, generates the high-speed finishing toolpath, verifies cutter clearance and remaining material, and outputs numerical control code or machine instructions. The invention may also be embodied in a machine tool controller configured to generate or modify the path in real time based on measured or simulated cutting conditions.

In use, a user selects an n-sided pocket or region to be finished and specifies machining parameters such as cutter type, diameter, corner radius, stepover, tolerance, feed rate, spindle speed, wall condition, and draft angle. The system analyzes the selected region, constructs a toolpath pattern that covers the region with smooth high-speed motion, and outputs a sequence of cutter positions and feed commands. The cutter then finishes the region while minimizing unnecessary air movement and maintaining a consistent surface finish along the pocket floor, walls, drafted surfaces, or transitions.

By reducing wasted cutter movement and by providing smooth, dynamically feasible transitions, the invention shortens machining cycle time, improves finish quality, reduces tool wear, and enables efficient finishing of n-sided pockets or regions that are difficult to machine using conventional offset or raster finishing strategies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an optimized cutter path algorithm for machining bounded regions with positive and negative drafted walls, especially for removing excess stock left by a previous larger diameter tool.
counterfactuals.output:
An optimized cutter-path algorithm for this problem is essentially a **draft-aware rest-machining algorithm**: it computes only the material that a previous, larger cutter could not reach, while respecting the true accessibility of positive and negative drafted walls.

Below is a practical algorithmic description.

---

## 1. Inputs

The algorithm assumes:

- A bounded machining region defined by:
  - outer boundary loops,
  - island loops,
  - floor elevation,
  - top elevation,
  - wall draft angle for each boundary segment.
- A previous cutter:
  - diameter,
  - corner radius / ball radius if applicable,
  - flute length and shank clearance if needed.
- A current smaller cutter.
- Machining parameters:
  - axial depth of cut,
  - stepover,
  - scallop tolerance,
  - climb/conventional direction,
  - safe height and linking rules.

The goal is to remove only the excess stock left by the larger cutter.

---

## 2. Represent the Drafted Region by Z-Slices

The bounded region is sliced into horizontal levels:

\[
z_0, z_1, z_2, \dots, z_n
\]

At each level, compute the actual 2D boundary of the drafted walls.

For a wall with draft angle \(\alpha\), the lateral shift of the boundary between a reference height \(z_f\) and the current height \(z\) is:

\[
d(z) = (z - z_f)\tan(\alpha)
\]

The sign of \(d(z)\) depends on whether the wall has positive or negative draft.

### Positive Draft

A positive drafted wall generally opens outward as height increases.

The accessible region normally becomes larger toward the top.

### Negative Draft

A negative drafted wall closes in toward the top.

The local slice at depth may look accessible, but the cutter may not be able to reach it because the tool body would collide with the narrower opening above.

Therefore negative draft requires a vertical accessibility test, not only a local offset test.

---

## 3. Compute Tool-Center Accessibility Regions

For each cutter and each slice level, compute the allowable cutter-center area.

Let:

- \(R_s(z)\) be the slice region at height \(z\),
- \(r_T\) be the effective cutter radius at the contact height,
- \(A_T(z)\) be the accessible cutter-center region for tool \(T\).

For a simple vertical end mill with no shaft collision concern:

\[
A_T(z) = \text{offset inward}(R_s(z), r_T)
\]

That is, the cutter center must remain at least one tool radius away from every wall.

For islands, the island boundaries are offset outward by the cutter radius.

---

## 4. Handle Negative Draft by Cumulative Accessibility

For negative draft, the cutter must pass through all upper slices before reaching the lower slice.

So the true accessible region is not merely the offset of the slice at depth \(z\). It is the intersection of all accessible openings above it:

\[
A_T(z) =
\bigcap_{\zeta=z}^{z_{top}}
\text{offset inward}(R_s(\zeta), r_T)
\]

This prevents the algorithm from creating gouging toolpaths in undercut or closing-wall areas that the tool cannot physically enter.

For tools with shanks, holders, or non-cylindrical cutter profiles, replace \(r_T\) with the effective radius of the cutter/shank at the corresponding height above the cutting point.

---

## 5. Compute Rest-Machining Regions

For each Z level, compute the region reachable by the new smaller tool but not reached by the previous larger tool.

Let:

\[
A_{new}(z)
\]

be the accessible cutter-center region for the current cutter, and

\[
A_{old}(z)
\]

be the accessible cutter-center region for the previous cutter.

The rest-machining center region is:

\[
R_{rest}(z) = A_{new}(z) - A_{old}(z)
\]

This region corresponds to the narrow bands, corners, and drafted-wall areas where the larger tool could not place its center, but the smaller tool can.

In practice, this Boolean subtraction is done with robust polygon clipping.

The result may contain:

- narrow strips along drafted walls,
- corner cleanup zones,
- regions near islands,
- pockets left by negative or mixed draft geometry,
- isolated cusps due to tool-diameter difference.

Very small regions below a machining tolerance may be discarded.

---

## 6. Generate Cutter Paths Inside the Rest Regions

For each connected component of \(R_{rest}(z)\), generate paths.

Common strategies are:

### A. Contour-Parallel Rest Paths

For wall cleanup, generate offsets parallel to the actual drafted boundary.

The first path lies approximately where the larger cutter stopped cutting, and the last path lies at the limit of the smaller tool’s accessibility.

The offset band width is roughly:

\[
r_{old} - r_{new}
\]

This is ideal for removing stock left along walls and islands.

### B. Pocket-Style Paths

If the rest region is wide enough, use a pocketing pattern:

- inward/outward offsets,
- adaptive clearing,
- spiral,
- trochoidal clearing if engagement must be limited.

### C. Corner Cleanup Paths

In tight internal corners, generate arcs or short loops centered on the corner bisector.

The path should be trimmed to the actual rest boundary to avoid re-cutting air.

---

## 7. Stepover and Scallop Control on Drafted Walls

For drafted walls, the effective scallop height depends on:

- cutter radius,
- wall angle,
- vertical step,
- lateral stepover.

A constant XY stepover may leave uneven scallops on steep draft angles.

A better method is to compute stepover based on surface scallop tolerance.

For a wall draft angle \(\alpha\), the stepover projected onto the wall surface is approximately:

\[
s_{surface} = \frac{s_{xy}}{\cos(\alpha)}
\]

So the XY stepover may be reduced as draft increases:

\[
s_{xy} = s_{target}\cos(\alpha)
\]

This keeps surface finish consistent on both shallow and steep drafted walls.

---

## 8. Avoid Gouging

Every candidate path should be verified against the part model.

For each cutter position:

1. Sweep the current cutter shape.
2. Check that it does not intersect the protected part geometry.
3. Check shank and holder clearance if required.
4. Confirm the swept volume lies inside the allowed stock-removal volume.

For negative draft, also verify the vertical entry path or approach move, because the cutter may fit at the target depth but collide while descending.

---

## 9. Optimize the Toolpath Order

After generating valid rest paths, optimize them.

Useful optimization steps include:

### Remove Redundant Cutting

Discard path segments where the previous cutter already removed material.

This can be done by comparing the new cutter sweep against the previous cutter sweep volume.

### Minimize Retracts

Build a graph of path segments or loops.

Each path has:

- start point,
- end point,
- cutting direction,
- required entry type,
- safe-linking constraints.

Then order the paths using a nearest-neighbor, 2-opt, or traveling-salesman-style heuristic.

### Prefer Continuous Cutting

Where safe, connect adjacent rest paths with:

- tangential links,
- small arcs,
- ramp links,
- stay-down transitions.

### Preserve Cutting Direction

For finishing drafted walls, maintain climb milling direction around the boundary.

For example:

- outer boundary loops may be cut clockwise,
- island loops may be cut counterclockwise,

depending on machine convention and coordinate orientation.

### Merge Similar Levels

If adjacent Z slices have nearly identical topology and offset distance, combine them into a single helical or ramping path instead of separate planar contours.

---

## 10. Stock Model Update

After each generated path or level, update the simulated stock model.

The algorithm should subtract the swept volume of the current cutter from the remaining stock.

This allows later operations to know exactly what material remains.

A voxel, Z-buffer, dexel, or boundary-representation stock model may be used.

---

## Simplified Pseudocode

```text
for each z_level in machining_depths:

    slice_region = compute_drafted_slice(part_region, z_level)

    new_access = compute_accessible_region(
                    slice_region,
                    current_tool,
                    z_level,
                    include_negative_draft_visibility = true)

    old_access = compute_accessible_region(
                    slice_region,
                    previous_tool,
                    z_level,
                    include_negative_draft_visibility = true)

    rest_region = boolean_difference(new_access, old_access)

    rest_region = remove_small_regions(rest_region, tolerance)

    for each connected_component in rest_region:

        if component_is_narrow_band(component):
            paths = generate_contour_parallel_paths(component)
        else:
            paths = generate_pocket_paths(component)

        paths = trim_paths_to_rest_region(paths, component)

        paths = smooth_and_filter(paths)

        paths = verify_against_part_geometry(paths, current_tool)

        add paths to level_toolpath_set

optimized_paths = optimize_path_order(level_toolpath_set)

simulate_and_update_stock(optimized_paths)

return optimized_paths
```

---

## Key Benefit

The main advantage of this algorithm is that it does not simply re-machine the whole bounded region with the smaller cutter. Instead, it computes:

\[
\text{material reachable by smaller cutter}
-
\text{material already reachable by larger cutter}
\]

while accounting for changing wall locations caused by positive and negative draft.

That produces shorter, safer, and more efficient cutter paths, especially around tapered walls, corners, islands, and restricted-access regions.
